utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday. Good morning to the accused. Good morning to Mr. Coric as well - he's not with us today but I hope he'll get well very soon. Good morning to the Defence counsel, to the representatives of the OTP, and to everyone assisting us in this case. Today we need to complete the cross-examination of the witness. Unless I'm mistaken, I believe that Mr. Bos has one hour and 15 minutes left, but I believe that Mr. Scott wants to address the Chamber. Mr. Scott, you wanted to raise an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to all those counsel and all those in the courtroom and those assisting us. Your Honour, very briefly, I don't anticipate with the time that we have today that we should have any significant time pressures I hope, but nonetheless I thought it would be best to raise these matters at the outset. Two matters related to upcoming witnesses. Your Honours, if I could just respectfully remind the Chamber and ask for the Chamber's assistance. On the -- I don't think that either one of these witnesses are protected, perhaps we could go into private session just for a moment just to be absolutely sure that I don't say something inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to counsel for that assistance. Your Honour, on the 9th of July of this year we filed a motion seeking an adequate summary for the Defence witness Borislav Puljic on the 9th of July, and that matter remains -- that motion remains pending. Likewise, on the 18th of August, 2008, a few weeks ago we filed a similar motion requesting an adequate summary for the witness Perica Jukic. Those two motions remain pending and of course Mr. Jukic is scheduled to testify next week, and I believe Mr. Puljic is scheduled to testify the following week. Therefore, it seems timely at least to bring those motions back before the Chamber's attention. Let me just briefly remind -- since the Chamber may not have looked at those motions, those written motions, that are pending recently, let me just briefly remind the Chamber of the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber issued a ruling regarding Mr. Jukic, Perica. This decision was duly recorded, and in this decision we requested a detailed summary from Mr. Karnavas in accordance with your application. Don't say that we didn't do anything because as soon as we receive a motion, as soon as it arrives on my desk, I examine the motion and the Trial Chamber reacts immediately. We issued a decision with respect to your motion. If you have not received the relevant document, Mr. Karnavas will tell us what it's all about. That's all I wanted to add to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It appears if I'm in error then I apologise to the Chamber or grant that it may be there's been an error among the Prosecution, and I take responsibility for that of course. It was our impression that that had not been resolved; if it has been then obviously it is a moot point. I would persist nonetheless with the Chamber's patience. I think the matter concerning Mr. Puljic, perhaps -- unless again I'm in error does remain outstanding. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please address this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, just as the Chamber's well aware by now and especially given what you, Mr. President, have just informed us in terms of the Chamber's dealing with the Jukic motion, the Tribunal law on this topic is really not ambiguous at all; it's quite clear that what Rule 65 ter requires is a summary of what the witness is actually expected to testify, not background, not he's held these positions, not simply a list of topics, the witness will testify about topic A, B, and C, but the actual evidence, the actual evidence, that the witness is expected to give, not that there was a meeting but that there was -- what the meeting was, what the meeting was about, what evidence the witness will give about that meeting. The Tribunal law is absolutely consistent on that. Report -- cases -- decisions from the Milosevic case, from the Mrksic case, from the Boskoski case, all of those cases have completely rejected witness summaries which simply give background and topics. They've been unanimous -- the decisions of the Trial Chambers in this Tribunal are unanimous in requiring fully adequate summaries so that both the opposing counsel, the opposing parties, and the Chamber can be more fully prepared to receive the evidence of that witness. Beyond that, Your Honour, I won't belabour it, but we would ask for the Chamber's assistance on ruling on our pending motion on Puljic, and again my apologies to the Chamber for being misinformed about the Jukic matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you will respond. Let me remind you that the Chamber has issued a ruling requesting that you submit to the Prosecution a detailed summary with respect to the witness who will testify next week. We gave the reasons for our decision. In that particular decision we relied on the case law of this Tribunal because several Trial Chambers of this Tribunal have clearly stated that the summary needs to be very detailed in order for the Prosecutor and also for the Judges. The Judges need to be able to prepare themselves properly before the testimony of the witness because under the Rules the Judges are allowed to put questions to the witness and they can only ask these questions if they have information available to them. That's why these summaries need to be very detailed and that's what we explained in our decision. If Mr. Scott takes the floor today about this point a few days before we hear your witness, it's because he has not received the summary. I don't know how things stand. Please can you clarify this for us, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Like the Prosecution, I must confess that I -- I frankly did not see the decision. Now, something must have slipped through the cracks. We apologise. We'll get on it. We understand that it may cause some inconvenience to the Prosecution. We will look at it. We will try to present a summary that obviously is in keeping with your order. Having said that, it seems to me what the Prosecution wishes for us to do is take statements and we're going -- it's like the dog chasing its tail. We're going back to that. You know, we don't take statements, we're not obligated to take statements, and when the Prosecution takes statements they don't take a question-and-answer statement; they normally summarize it the way they wish it, and a lot of times the statement doesn't contain information -- all of the information they intend to put on before the -- when the witness testifies. So I do feel that slowly what the Trial Chamber is doing is going through the back door and forcing the Prosecution -- forcing the Defence, contrary to the Rules, to provide statements. That's what's happening here. You may be shaking your head, Judge Trechsel, but it appears to be the case. We do provide summaries. And may I say, Judge Trechsel, may I say that in the previous trial that I had, I submitted similar summaries and then prior to the commencement of the trial, Judge Liu, who was presiding the case, when he thought that a particular summary was insufficient he requested it at that time. In other words, the Trial Chamber looked at the summaries early prior to the Defence case, not in the middle of the Defence case, and it seems that slowly -- and I know that you're one of the movers and the shakers behind this, pushing us to give not just detailed summaries but essentially summaries that effect -- that are in a sense statements. And it becomes very difficult at this stage of the proceedings. I mean logistically, with all due respect, you have any idea of what it's like, especially when you keep putting demands on the Defence to give you binders in the order in which the documents are presented. We did this with the last witness. It took three working days of one person to do that on a minor witness where there was only one binder or a binder and a half. So while I don't object to providing more and more detail, in the middle of the trial it's becoming more and more complex and more and more difficult, especially now when we're going to have the Prosecution demanding that we file our motions with respect to evidence that we're trying to get in by way of motion. We put our case before you. Obviously the Prosecution wants to jam. We heard Mr. Stringer: This is a game. This is how the game they want -- is supposed to be played. That's how they see it. This is no longer now a mission to see if, in fact, we can get to the truth and if the Prosecution can meet its burden. And I think that we're being overburdened by these demands over and over again that go beyond, in my opinion, even the case law. Now, we will provide a greater summary, but there comes a point where that summary is in a sense is nothing less than a statement. And if the Trial Chamber wants a statement, let the trial demand -- that the Trial Chamber demand a statement from us so that then we can seek an appeal on this issue. But I do -- I must confess, we provided you with sufficient information which at the commencement of the trial you thought was fine; otherwise, you would have ordered differently. And now we're doing it witness by witness and it's going to continue because the Prosecution, no matter how much you give them, they're going to want more. That's the nature of the beast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, you're talking along the motto that attack is the best defence. And while we ask for information you hyper state that, and in order to fight any reproach in advance you suppose that we ask much more than we actually do, which is a well-known tactic. But I think it's not quite fair. We have not asked for statements but for nothing more than the case law demands. And I think you have actually agreed to that and I think one could leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I thought we presented what the case law demands. We will provide some more. The witness will be coming in today, a day early. We are scheduled to meet with the witness on Saturday. Hopefully we will try to present and give the Prosecution something by tomorrow, you know, hopefully by the beginning of tomorrow. In case they want additional information we can meet with the witness. But you must understand, we don't have the luxury of a large team in the field, and sometimes it's not until the witness comes here that we really have an opportunity to go over the documents with the witness. As you can see this is a heavily documented case. We don't -- we cannot demand three or four days of a witness in the field prior to trial. Most of them don't want to give us more than one or two hours, and that's why in some instances what we do present is what we believe and what we think the evidence will be at that time. So we will try to present more, and hopefully we'll satisfy the Prosecution. But we're doing the best that we can and that's the bottom line and that's what I'm trying to convey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Scott later on but before that one question. With respect to Mr. Puljic, I'm being reminded by the Legal Officer that before the -- before recess we had requested an additional summary from you with respect to that witness. This information, this request, was sent to you by the Chamber. I can understand that you may have forgotten that because of the amount of work you have to do, but I believe you will now be able to provide this additional information to us. Secondly, we are not requesting you to provide statements. Of course that would be ideal, but we are fully aware of the fact that considering the amount of time you have at your disposal it's impossible for you to start taking statements. On the other hand, and I've already stated that many times, I said that a few weeks ago, what the Chamber wants based on a very detailed summary is what is -- what the witness will be testifying about in order for the Chamber to prepare itself properly, and that's the same for the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor wants to prepare for the cross-examination. Of course you've produced summaries, I don't deny it, but these summaries are rather concise, are rather short, and they should be detailed, developed, and it's in your interest because when we have a detailed summary in front of us then we have a clearer idea about what -- why the witness is coming to testify, and we understand what you are trying to establish. It's in our interest to provide detailed summaries to us because through these summaries you present our case, and if you give us only a very short summary then we do not quite know what the witnesses will be talking about. That applies to the witness we'll be hearing next week because after reading his summary there are still a lot of open questions about him, but we'll have answers to these questions because you've said that you are going to provide a more detailed summary with respect to that witness. We are perfectly aware of the problems you have. You've spent the entire week with us, and during all this time of course you can't meet with your witnesses. I'm fully aware of that. I know you're up to a very difficult task because you do not have the same resources as the Prosecutor; I'm perfectly aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With Mr. Puljic, Your Honour, we simply put that on the back burner because he was -- the order was changed and we're just trying to keep our heads above the water, but we will provide something for Mr. Puljic and anyone else following that as quickly as we can. The Prosecution should rest assure that in the future if they just want to pick up the phone or send us a message we will respond to that. So -- and again, my apologies for not seeing the decision. I take full responsibility in that. Somehow it fell through the cracks. I wasn't aware, otherwise I certainly would not have ignored it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, I'm sure -- I'm absolutely sure that you're going to do your best. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Only a moment and I won't belabour it further. Your Honour, Mr. President, you and Judge Trechsel have made the comments better than -- I'm sure better than I can make them. I appreciate the Chamber's additional guidance. I do want to note, however, because I do agree with Judge Trechsel, that the high hyperbole is really not necessary. The Prosecution simply asks for what the law -- what the Rules and Tribunal Rules require. There's nothing novel or even creative about the Prosecution's argument, frankly. It's exactly what the Rules require. Rule 65 ter requires these summaries not be provided just a day or two before the witness appears, notwithstanding whatever difficulties there might be, but it's quite difficult in saying that at the time the Defence make their pre-trial filings after the close of the Prosecution's case and before the commencement of the Defence case, the Pre-Trial Judge shall require them to file the following, including a summary of the facts on what each witness will testify. And again, Tribunal -- the Tribunal case law is quite clear on it. So the Prosecution is not pushing beyond -- asking for anything more, more extensive, or belabouring or putting more burdens on the Defence than what the law and the Rules require. Second brief point, Your Honour, in terms of the format or approach that the Prosecution has taken, let me just briefly remind the courtroom for purposes of the record that indeed when the summaries were initially filed and some of the pre-trial and pre-Defence conferences and hearings that Prosecution did raise - because we did review preliminarily the summaries provided - at that time, I'm sure the record will show, that we did raise our concerns that a number of the summaries appeared inadequate. So it's not fair to say that we're just raising this on a piecemeal basis. However, the direction we received at that time was that it would be better to take them on a case-by-case basis as the issues arose. Therefore, the Prosecution has followed the Chamber's guidance on that and will indeed -- as Mr. Karnavas says, we will indeed continue to do so whenever in the course of preparing for a witness we review the summaries again on a case-by-case basis and -- and do conclude in our respectful submission that the summaries are not sufficient. So I just wanted to make those points clear for the record, but beyond that I appreciate the Chamber's guidance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think that one thing Mr. Karnavas said makes a lot of sense, namely, that you take contact directly and negotiate and treat directly with the Defence team. It may be other teams later on, so as not to take too much time of the Chamber because we are 20 minutes after beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. We've done that on some occasions. I think Mr. Karnavas would confirm that in the past couple of months we've done more of that. We'll try to do more. Sometimes -- sometimes it appears that filing a pleading and discussing it with the Chamber sometimes becomes necessary, but I take on board your comments, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the witness brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Please accept the Chamber's apologies, but we had to deal with a procedural matter. That's why you had to wait for 20 minutes before entering the courtroom. Please accept our apologies. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Bos, who is going to proceed with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, last -- yesterday we left off with a quote that I was going to read out to you from the Kordic case in relation to the camps, and I'll read the quote again. It's from the 7th of June, 2000, transcript page 20684 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could read -- the question could be read as well because the question goes then with the answer. I was going to object yesterday, but we ran out of time, so question and then answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I will have to get the transcript then. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll start with the question. "Q. Just so I understand, is it possible, to your way of thinking, that to feed thousands of detainees, bus them, to house them, could be done spontaneously or would it have had to come from some plan?" And then your answer is: "I'm not denying -- and I already said that -- that at local level there were such treatments of civilian, non-Croat populations. This cannot be justified by war operations, and there is no basis for that in the legislation of Herceg-Bosna. I am not saying that someone did or did not issue an order to establish such centres. "Nevertheless, the nature of the work that I did was such that I was not in contact with that. I'm just saying that I don't know whether there was such an order or not." Mr. Perkovic, do you recall this evidence that you gave in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then, would you agree that here you admit that civilian non-populations [sic] were kept in detention centres and that there was no legal basis for that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the fact that those centres existed, but in my line of work I did not have to deal with those problems, and I was aware of some cases at the local level where such measures were taken against civilians. That's what I said in my evidence eight years ago, and I say that again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which HVO detention centres did you know were functioning at the time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about centres such as Dretelj, Heliodrom, Gabela, they were being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who do you think would have been responsible for running these camps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know that because it was not my job. I was not aware of the legal status of those centres, whether those were prisons or prisoner-of-war camps. So I didn't know that. I can't answer your question, therefore, because I was not aware of its status and I didn't know who was supposed to be in charge of running those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the treatment of prisoners at these detention centres was ever discussed at HVO government meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this topic was discussed at at least one session that I attended, and I cannot rule out the possibility that it was discussed at other meetings, too. But at a session of the HVO, I think it was in August 1993, this problem was discussed and after a debate about the conditions in those centres it was agreed that they were unsatisfactory in terms of the accommodation, food, and all the other issues that affect the people who were there, and the conclusion was reached to take a number of measures to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the minutes of some of these meetings. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 03560 in your binder. These are the minutes of the 19th of July, 1993, the 46th Session of the HVO government meeting. Now, Mr. Perkovic, if we look at the document we'll see on the first page the persons present at this meeting, and your name appears in that list of names as well. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention now to item number 7 of this document which is on page 4 of the English version. Let me just read out what's been stated here. "After a discussion of the request of the HVO of Capljina municipality to relocate prisoners and a discussion of the status and accommodation condition of prisoners and persons in isolation with the aim of improving their accommodation conditions and overcoming the newly arisen situation, unanimous approval was given to adopt the following ..." And then there's a list with two conclusions, and I'll just read out the first conclusion: "Secure accommodation conditions, material, and medical support for prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Conventions relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War. "If the existing accommodation conditions are not satisfactory, the head of the defence department of justice and general administration in coordination with the defence department and the defence -- and the department of interior shall designate new sites and transfer prisoners of war. "The defence department shall be in charge of their stay at the new sites." Now, sir, just focus your attention on what's being said here under item 7. It talks about overcoming the newly arisen situation. Do you recall what had happened, why -- and what kind of newly arisen situation had arose? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in light of the date when this session took place, it was the 19th of July, I assume that the new development can only have to do with the war-related events in that area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the Capljina municipality. I'm not aware of any other circumstances that might be described as new developments, the new circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And looking at the conclusion under number 1, would you agree that reading the second sentence of that conclusion, it gives responsibility to the departments of defence, justice, and interior in case the accommodation conditions of detention centres are not satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let's look at another document which is P 04841, which is again minutes of a HVO government meeting of 6 September 1993. You have it? Again, under the list of names you see that your name is listed as well, so would you agree that you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let me read out to you the first two paragraphs under item 1. "On the basis of verbal reports and insight gained into the matter of executing punishments and the condition of detention of persons captured as active-duty and reserve enemy forces and persons preparing an armed rebellion, the situation was declared unsatisfactory and harmful to the reputation [Realtime transcript read in error "representation"] and interests of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. "It was also concluded that the responsibility for the persons present -- for the present situation does not lie with the HVO of the government of the Croatian community -- of the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However, in order to avoid the situation being used in ways that are adverse to the political and other interests of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna," I should say, "... valid principles of international law, of law and international humanitarian law need to be observed in executing punishments and implementing other measures." Now, first of all, was this the meeting that you were referring to earlier when you said that there was a meeting in August about these camps, is this the meeting you were actually referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was referring to this meeting. I couldn't recall the exact month, but this was an item on the agenda of the HVO HZ HB or the government of the HR HB that dealt with this issue, this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it says here in the second paragraph that -- there's a denial of the responsibility for the conditions of the HVO detention as to the responsibility of the HVO government. We've just saw the other minutes where we clearly see that there was a responsibility for various minister -- or departments within the HVO on the conditions of detention, and now here we see that it's being stated that -- yeah, that there is no responsibility. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a correction on the record. On line 19 it is -- one reads: "It is harmful to the representation and interest of the Croatian community," it's not representation, it's reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see two important things from the minutes here, first, that the HVO discusses those problems on the basis of oral reports; in other words, there is no paper trail, there are no documents that were used as a basis for the discussion at this meeting. And I would like to remind you that in accordance with the Rules of Procedure of the HVO, the HVO departments were duty-bound to provide written materials for the discussion at the meetings of the HVO. And it is quite clear to me from this that the jurisdiction was not that of the HVO HZ HB, but it is obviously within the jurisdiction of the local authorities, municipal authorities, the municipal HVOs. And in this context it is logical to conclude, I say, that the HVO HZ HB was not responsible for the situation as it was up until that time, but taking as our starting point that the document that we had seen just a little while ago, where the HVO indicates that there are violations of the Geneva Conventions pertaining to war, the conclusion that is logical is that since the local authorities are doing nothing to rectify the situation the HVO, as a guarantor of the compliance with those conventions, takes it upon itself to perform all those tasks that have to be done in order to rectify the situations -- the situation and bring it in line with those conventions to improve the conditions of life of those people. And to me it seems completely consistent and completely responsible conduct on the part of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in a situation where the local authorities are in violation of the international regulations and the regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, in your answer you keep focusing on the responsibility of the local authorities, but as we have just seen in July -- one month earlier there is a discussion with the -- in the HVO government about the conditions of these detention centres. And then clearly several departments are being given assignments in relation to the conditions of these detention centres. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question, Your Honour. It assumes facts that are not really in evidence. If you look at the previous document, those heads of departments are being asked to look into it, not that they're responsible for the conditions, try to find alternative accommodations. So I think if he's going to quote, go back to the document, quote the actual language, let's keep the facts as they are based on the documents and not based on interpretations by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move back to Exhibit 3560, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to understand this well. When you talk about local authorities, you mean municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How about a civilian prison, whose responsibility is it to manage it? Is it the municipal authorities when it comes to housing, food, et cetera, or was it a central state prerogative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before answering your question I would just like to ask you to clarify. Do you mean a prison or a centre? Because a prison is a place where criminal sanctions are enforced and here we're talking about the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, tell us what in your view is a prison, provide us with your definition of a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A prison is an institution where -- where persons who were convicted in a final judgement and were given sentence that was upheld on appeal serve their sentences or a place where persons are detained in the course of the investigation. That is a prison. A centre is an institution where persons are kept in detention, those persons who are prisoners of war during the war and they are put there but no criminal proceedings have been instituted against them and no sentences have been imposed on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the basis of those definitions, please answer my question. My question was whose responsibility was it to manage those prisons or centres, was it the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The responsibility to make sure that the penalties and sentences were imposed across prisons according to the regulations Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as far as prisons were concerned fell to the president of the Supreme Court in any of these areas, as that was for civilian prisons. As for the military prisons, it was the responsibility of the president of the higher military court or the supreme military court, the responsibility in terms of sentences being carried out and penalties imposed. As for detention centres for prisoners of war, as far as Herceg-Bosna's regulations were concerned, these centres for the detention of war prisoners according to the regulations were under the charge of the justice minister and the defence department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos, I would have many questions but in light of the time remaining I'd rather Mr. Bos carries on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Perkovic, I asked you to move back to Exhibit 3560. I don't know if you have that in front of you. Just let's look again at the text under the conclusion of number 1 where it says: "In the existing accommodation conditions, if existing accommodation are not satisfactory, the head of the defence -- the head of the department of justice and general administration in coordination with the defence department and department of interior shall designate new sites and transfer prisoners of war." And then: "The defence department shall be in charge of stay at their new sites." Now, clearly when it says here "shall be in charge of stay at their new sites," you will agree that there's responsibility of the defence department in relation to this? And maybe it goes back to your answer to Judge Antonetti, that the defence department was responsible for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is only conditional, as you see, it is not being stated outright. It reads: "If the conditions are not satisfactory," so this is something that is up to the defence department. Then at a meeting of the HVO of the HZ HB they agreed to this conclusion, but only in a conditional sense, this is being an assumption, because that was the responsibility of that department and then that department should probably know. On the other hand, if you look at the introduction to this particular item you see that the municipal HVO of Capljina is asking for prisoners to be moved. Now, the question I'm asking myself because of this is why is it the HVO of Capljina municipality asking for this, why not another HVO? And why would that be a problem for the HVO of Capljina municipality if this is the responsibility of the defence department or some other department of the HVO HZ HB? Why would someone worry about someone else's business when at the time in this area everyone was encountering so many problems of their own without being able to deal with them in an effective manner? If you look at all of this what becomes obvious is that by July, by the 19th of July, 1993, at least as far as this centre is concerned, the institutions and organs of the HVO of HZ HB had no insight into the work of this centre or any powers over the work of this centre. Had that not been the case, it would have been necessary for the HVO to discuss this at a government meeting, all these problems, and it wouldn't have been necessary to take over from someone who was obviously performing this task in a very poor manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But it's exactly the point. Isn't it true that in these minutes in fact what's happening here is that the various departments of the Croatian government are taking over and that's exactly what it says here: "The defence department shall be in charge of their stay at the new sites ..." Is that not what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have to intervene. I'm sorry. I don't think this is a fair way to ask this question. Mr. Bos gets an answer that he doesn't like and then he's insinuating something that is not actually there. It's exactly what the witness said, should the conditions be found to be unsatisfactory and if another location is found, then it will be the defence department. That's this point. And then the next conclusion before the setting up of this work group. Therefore, I think that the answer [as interpreted] should be re-asked in a way that's fair and in keeping with what the transcript actually reflects. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please clarify this. Ms. Nozica says that in the witness' answer it had been said that if the situation had been such and such, so it was hypothetical, and you seem to make a statement out of this hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question this -- how do you interpret the line: "The defence department shall be in charge of their stay at the new sites ..." in this -- in these minutes? How should I interpret this sentence or how do you interpret this sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the enactments of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna when it was first founded and when it started exercising its powers, one of the most notable statements by the HVO and by the Croatian institutions was that about their intention of complying with all the international rules and regulations, including the Geneva Conventions. This was a situation where at the local level the HVO realized that certain actions, certain forms of behaviour, were not in keeping with all of that. A situation, as I've been telling you for the last two days, in which the HVO did not have the political power to change, or rather, to replace the municipal council of Capljina's HVO, it is a logical conclusion that the HVO should use its institutions and its departments to take up this particular job and make sure that the guarantees previously granted were being complied with in order to fix and improve in a way the overall situation and bring it up to speed with international standards. Against that background, I understand this initiative towards the HVO but also the readiness and the sense of obligation on the part of the HVO. When we talk about this centre, we're talking about a centre that was in Capljina municipality, in Capljina municipal area, and then to take this responsibility in order to improve the overall situation. If you look at all these documents, it follows that the HVO and the HVO departments have no powers over that up until the period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I just -- one final matter on this because -- so you're sort of concluding from reading this document that it's the HVO Capljina municipality who would have been responsible for the camp there, but looking at item 7 does it read anywhere that the Capljina municipality is actually responsible for the camp? It says here: "At the request by the HVO of Capljina municipality to relocate prisoners ..." It doesn't say anywhere that the municipality of Capljina is actually responsible for these prisoners, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I object to the form of the question. It's not whether this document says. It's what the witness -- his knowledge of the events. If you look at the last two or three pages, Your Honours, and I have -- I've sat quiet, this question has been asked and answered. He indicated that these were municipal activities. He indicated that it was under the municipality. He indicates that here Capljina is being called -- called upon based on item 7. He's also talking about at this point in time, because of the irregularities, the HVO HZ HB and the heads of -- and its departments are now going to try to resolve this issue; in other words, try to take it over, that's why they're saying, Check it out. If it's necessary, find new accommodations and you, that is, the HVO departments, will be responsible. It's all there. It's been said, it's been done. You know, I don't see why we're going over this over and over again. And I would suspect that, Judge Trechsel, you may -- might wish to intervene and say this has been asked and answered. I don't see how you can try to take something out of context. Look at the past three or four pages. The answer is right there. I don't mind. We have until, you know, 1.45 as far as I'm concerned, and the gentleman can stay on Monday if that's necessary, but I think that he got his answer, we should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm intending to move on. I'm really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos -- very well, yes. Witness, to clarify this, from what I understood you stated that the HVO municipal authorities - and you provided us with the Capljina example - to some extent were a bit at a loss which accounts for a certain number of problems. And when the central HVO realized this, it was then decided to entrust the department of defence with the department of justice the task of taking care of those problems. You interpreted this because politically the HVO head did not have enough power to dismiss the municipal authorities, so the only way out was to take care of the problem themselves. Have I summarized the way you have told us you experienced things at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, you have just mentioned a number of things that I believe are important. If I may please be allowed to comment. Many members of the HVO of the HZ HB, including myself, never had an opportunity up until this period of time to see or to visit or to have any sort of information at all available to them about any of these centres. Therefore, when we talk about this period you see that the HVO are having discussions here based on the verbally transmitted information, there is nothing in writing. Then again, I said two days ago that it was beyond doubt that the HVO had normative powers to replace or disband any of its municipal bodies, any of the municipal HVOs; but I also said that it is my deepest conviction that the HVO of the HZ HB did not have the political power to do that and I corroborated that by citing several examples explaining - without wanting to repeat myself - why I said what I said. And thirdly, and this is very important, when we talk about the conditions under which people were put up at a time of war, under which people were accommodated, it is very important to bear in mind the context at the time when this happens. I personally witnessed for myself how Croat refugees were being put up at a farm in Livno. Up until several days previously, there were cattle and livestock being kept there. The stables obviously had been scrubbed up, but there was still very strong smell of ammonia in those rooms over there. Obviously this was not an ideal solution, not even under the circumstances, not even at the time, but then again I'm telling you the question of accommodation at the time and in that context was a very relative question because it depended on a lot of things. At that time and in that situation the conclusion just imposed itself. One had to run certain checks and that's why this is being put in the conditional, the conditions being what they are. And if the conditions are satisfactory, then we must do this or we must do that. And then I'm telling you about the entire context and the entire conclusion, and it's my deepest conviction, based on the overall conclusion reached by the HVO, it follows that the HVO, or most of the members of the HVO, don't understand the overall situation in the sense of the conditions under which those centres were working and under which the people would stay who were being put up at those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of your question, if you look at under the agenda item 7, it says, "any other business," and then look at item 7 itself, and I think there lies perhaps part of the answer to your question as well. You can quite clearly see that it wasn't on the agenda; it's something that just popped up. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies, I do have a general objection, a very brief one though. This is something to do with Mr. Bos's examination. Yesterday, the Chamber allowed my learned friend to ask questions about this subject matter, but it was pointed out - and this is at transcript page 31959 - that he should cross-examine in the manner of direct examination and mind the way he was putting his questions and not do a proper cross-examination on this particular subject matter. Maybe I'm under the wrong impression, but I'm listening to him today and what I think I'm seeing is a textbook cross-examination with all the leading questions and everything that follows from that. This is my general objection and could the Chamber consider my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With respect to your objection, as far as I'm concerned - but I believe that my fellow Judges share my view - if you look at Rule 90(H)(ii): "A party may be allowed to put questions that go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief," Rule 90(H)(iii). Mr. Bos raised matters that had not been dealt with during the examination-in-chief of this witness. But since the witness was in a position to deal with matters that are raised in the indictment, the Trial Chamber allowed Mr. Bos to deal with these issues and the witness answered the questions put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I entirely agree with what the President has just said. In addition, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic recalls a rule that we have much discussed and with reference to American law -- I see Mr. Karnavas remembers the same way I do; and indeed, the Chamber has determined that in this area non-directive questions must be asked and no leading questions. So I recall this, if you are outside the realm covered by direct, no leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours, I'll take that on board, but I now intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, let's move to another topic, which is the creation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Now, if I understand your evidence, is it correct that you worked on the founding document of this institution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you -- can you tell us again on how this -- how this came about. Who did ask you to work on this document and with whom did you work on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days before the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the HVO HZ HB, Mr. Prlic, summoned me and a number of other people to a meeting. At this meeting there were Kresimir Zubak, Miroslav Djidic, Mr. Zoran Buntic, I'm not sure if there was anyone else, and I. There were a total of four or five people at the meeting altogether. At the meeting we were told that the final touches were being added to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan which was a new peace plan at the time, envisaging a new solution for the internal organization of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This solution meant primarily the establishment of a union of the three republics. Against that background, we were supposed to pave the way - we the Croatian side - for the implementation of this plan. We were given a brochure, or rather, a document containing the plan. We were also told that we didn't have much time and that we should do this practically on an ad hoc basis over the next 24 hours. When drafting these documents we were told we should use the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan as a reference for everything that we did, and that was contained in the brochure. So this was the basic information that we got and we state our play in a bid to finish all of that. This was a day before the establishment because when the founding session began and the delegates were there and all those who were invited to take part in this founding session when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established, the work began before those people were given the documents because they were still being printed. It wasn't until an hour later that they came. It was perhaps an hour after the close of that session that the materials were distributed to everyone with these three decisions, the decision of setting up the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the decision to establish a Chamber of Deputies, and then I think there was something else, so the three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one clarification, on line 15 he says -- it says here: "Perhaps an hour after the close of that session." And my colleague tells me that Mr. Perkovic says, "Perhaps an hour before the" -- "after the opening of the session," not the close of the session but the opening of the session. So perhaps we could get a clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So those materials we distributed about an hour after the opening of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've just explained why this document related to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was drafted, but you kept saying "we" or "they." Who was it? Who told you that as part of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan three republics would be set up? Who told you that? Who told you that? Because of that very fact the Republic of Herceg-Bosna needed to be established and that's the reason why you were asked to draft this text, but who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a while ago, and as I shall repeat, we were summoned to the meeting by Mr. Prlic. As for the plan itself, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, we got this plan in the form of a brochure and we were told by Mr. Prlic that when drafting those documents we should take into account the fact that they had to be in keeping with the plan. When I say "we," I mean the group that was supposed to prepare to draft those documents, and I told you who the group comprised in addition to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it correct that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established on the 28th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at that session. I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would you also agree - and I think you already testified to that - that this -- that on the day it was established there wasn't yet an agreement signed in relation to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, so that this document was established -- this document was adopted, whereas the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan had not been signed. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's true. As far as I know, the plan has not been signed to this very day. Now that you've raised this, we lawyers would say that the matter of establishing the republic against the background of this plan was the same as the previous issue because the implementation of the plan was impossible unless you had the three republics. As for the draft plan, that's exactly the kind of solution that it envisages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But is it not true, Mr. Perkovic, that in late August there was still some very controversial issues in relation to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that had not yet been solved, and maybe for the Croatian party it was all okay but not necessarily for the Muslims and the Serbs? Would you agree with me that on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, I did not take part in the negotiations and the drafting of that plan and I'm not aware of any issues that remained unsolved at that time. So I didn't know that at the time and I don't know it now. As far as we were concerned, this plan was tabled as a plan of the international community, backed by the major powers and the Croatian side and the other two sides were asked to be cooperative when it came to accepting this plan. I don't think that this cooperative attitude that envisaged the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna too should now be taken against the Croatian side, because let me remind you the Croatian side is the only side that signed all of the peace agreements in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, would it surprise you if I said an important reason for the Bosniaks not to eventually sign this plan was actually their fear for the creation of a Bosnian-Croat mini state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was -- that that was one of the reasons that they didn't want to sign this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. On what basis does he say that? It's like me saying the reason they didn't sign it is Izetbegovic wants to establish an Islamic state based on the declaration and based on his involvement with certain radical elements, Islam elements, such as those that he was importing the Mujahedin and the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- from Iran, from Pakistan, from Afghanistan, and so on. That would be pure speculation on my part. Now, if I can back it up with facts that's another thing, but at this point he's asking the gentleman to speculate on what he believes is his theory and what the Muslim side feared at the time. I don't think that's a proper question. It goes beyond the facts that have been established and I object to the line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's evidence on the record from the Ribicic expert report which exactly states that and that's why I was mentioning this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Ribicic expert report deals with the constitutionality; it has nothing to do with whether Izetbegovic was fearing a state within a state. And may I remind, Ribicic never met with any of the key players and didn't even know the existence of Akmadzic, Jure Pelivan, and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the witness has just explained why the republic was established. He told us that this was within the context of the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan and that Mr. Prlic asked them to draft this document in accordance with the documents coming out of that international conference. The witness has therefore answered in a very precise and accurate manner. The Prosecutor has another theory, and he puts that theory to the witness. The witness may say, I don't agree with you, sir, because I've already answered and I don't agree. So no need to raise an objection. We are wasting time, and your own witness is saying some things that go against the case of the Prosecution. So that's one point in your favour. Why do you object? Why do you want prevent the witness answering the Prosecutor's question? I don't understand. So, Witness, the Prosecutor has just asked you a question. Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question. I do apologise, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's going to repeat it. Please repeat your question, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Perkovic, would it surprise you to say that an important reason for the Bosniaks not to eventually sign the Owen Peace Plan was their actual fear for the creation of a Bosnian-Croat mini state in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina have their fears. Perhaps this is a fear that Bosniaks have. Croats have their own fears. They are afraid of a unitary, centralised state. Serbs probably have their own fears. But judging by the fact that the Bosniak side agreed and accepted the Republika Srpska as a constituent entity, I really can't see your point because if they were not afraid of one entity, the Serb entity, why would they have to be afraid of another entity which would be smaller and which would have smaller population than the other one, the Croat one? So I can't really accept this claim that there was some fear. I think it was just purely political calculation at work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just said something that I'd never heard before. I'm very curious by nature, and it strikes me. You said that the Bosniaks had accepted the Republika Srpska as a constitutional entity. On what basis can you say that because it's the first time I've heard this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim this on the basis of Mr. Izetbegovic's signature on the Dayton Peace Agreement which stipulated that there should be two entities within Bosnia and Herzegovina and one of them is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that happened at the Dayton Peace Agreements and not before. I understood it happened before. But thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, maybe we can have a look at the founding documents, which is P 04611. Now, what I'd like to do is go over the text of this document with you, and we'll start with the preamble and then in particular the third paragraph of the preamble. And I think you referred to this paragraph as well in your examination-in-chief. Would you agree with me that this third paragraph confirms that this document was in anticipation of the peace agreement? It talks about transferring a part of their constitutive right to the future federation of the republic and in the end it says, "As shall be regulated by ..." so would you agree that this was all in anticipation of the peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 3 of the preamble speaks about the readiness of the Croatian side to transfer some of the powers to the common state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But do you agree it talks about the future federation, so it does here confirm that such a federation doesn't exist yet. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a mention of the future union, not federation, in -- federation is a different kind of a system, but at any rate this paragraph speaks about the readiness of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna where -- that it is ready to transfer a part of its rights to this future state. And this state should be defined in terms of its internal structure and constitution in line with this plan that was on the table at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the preamble number 4, and I was a bit curious about this particular preamble. It reads as follows: "Pursuant to the political decisions of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the legitimate representative of the political will of the Croatian people ..." Now, can you explain what was the purpose of this provision? It's the last preamble before the actual decision.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand you. I can't see any political party being mentioned in the preamble, including the Croatian Democratic Union in this document -- this document has nothing to do with the Croatian Democratic Party. I don't know if I understood the interpretation correctly because I was told that you are talking about the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I hope this is not a translation issue, but at least in the English version, and I'm referring to the fourth paragraph of the preamble, it clearly refers to the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to political decisions of the ... It's right above when the basic decision is ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the last item in the fourth paragraph. I do apologise. Yeah, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So my question is, first of all: Why is there here a reference to the Croatian Democratic Union in this preamble? How do we need to interpret this preamble paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union was the political party that at the first multi-party elections won, having garnered most of the Croat votes. And on the basis of the number of the representatives it had in the BH parliament, it derived its legitimacy from there, and when it came to passing key, basic, fundamental decisions about the fate of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, on the basis of their victory at the first multi-party elections the representatives of the HDZ concluded that they did have the legitimacy to represent and defend Croat interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So -- but if Bosnian Croats in Bosnia would be members of other Croatian parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, like you were a member of the SDP, how would these Croats look at a preamble like this? Would that not be a -- I'm still trying to find out why this provision was being put here. Didn't you want to represent all Bosnian Croats in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, am quite unhappy with this wording but I cannot contest the fact that at the time the Croatian Democratic Union did have the legitimacy to represent the political interests of the Croat people on the basis of their success at the first multi-party elections, as I've already noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's half past 10.00. We need to break for 20 minutes, and after the break the registrar will tell me how much time you have left, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's resume the hearing. This is not what I said. The Chamber had prepared a draft ruling but it was not recorded because we had to -- prepared a reply to take place in September. We were waiting for replies to be provided on September 2nd, so the decision or the ruling was not taken, so the ruling was not recorded because there was no reply. This being said, I reiterate my request to Mr. Karnavas to provide us as soon as possible with a detailed summary. Let's proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's not possible to follow the transcript what Your Honour has just said because we didn't get interpretation of the first bit. So what Your Honour has just said there on the transcript isn't linked -- we do actually know what it's about but it's very obscure on the transcript because when Your Honour first started speaking there wasn't any interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. I just wanted to make a correction, correct some things I had already said on the ruling on the summaries. I said before the break that a ruling had been made and recorded, but after checking this it appears that we had prepared a draft ruling but that ruling was not recorded because we were waiting for a reply by the 2nd of September, but we didn't receive that reply on the 2nd of September and we forgot about it. So there is no ruling. But still, we ask Mr. Karnavas to send his detailed summary as soon as possible. Let's resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I just want to ask you one more question about the reference to the Croatian Democratic Union in the preamble. What I would like to know from you, was the -- the Croatian Democratic Union referenced here, was this the one that was the one that was in place when the free elections took place in 1990 and that part -- time the party was headed by Mr. Kljuic, or is this the Croatian Democratic Union of August 1993 where Mr. Mate Boban was leading the party? How should I interpret this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the Croatian Democratic Union which was unified at that time, a political party, which as far as I know from Mr. Kljuic up until Mr. Boban did not change it statute and did not change its political platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move to Article 4 of the text, and I'll read out the text and then I'll ask you a question about this. "The sovereignty of the republic shall be indivisible, inalienable, and nontransferable, and the republic may exercise certain rights and duties in the joint bodies of the federation of the republic. "The republic shall join the federation of republics freely." Now, I would like to focus my attention on the word "freely." What is the meaning of that word in this context? Does it mean that in fact the Croatian republic would have a right in order -- either to leave the union or even not enter the union? How should I interpret the word "freely" here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, freely in this context means what the word freely means in everyday parlance, and that means that the republic shall join on the basis of the freely expressed will of the legitimate representatives of the Croat people, and as you've already seen on the basis of these decisions they are -- they sit in the parliament. And here only the acceding to a union is talked about, not leading a union. I assume that if the option of leaving the union were also considered at the time this word could have been put in paragraph 2 of article 4, but we can see that there is no such word, which means that there was no such intention either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, but you would agree with me that if you read the text it does mean that if the republic would decide not to join the union that this line actually allows them to do so; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your question -- well, I've already told you why the Croatian republic was established. I told you why this article was framed in this manner. Had there not been the intention to join this union there would not have been any need to put such an article in, and there would have been no need to pass this legal instrument constituting this entity at all. There is no purpose for you to define your own obligation in a legal instrument, and at the same time to be calculating and to plan that you would not comply with this obligation. It is -- there is this clear intention to join a union of republics, and this intention was confirmed by the signature of the legitimate representatives of the Croat side, the signature that they affixed to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's move then to Article 9 which talks about the coat of arms and a flag and an anthem. Now, we know that the Croatian community had its own flag and had its own coat of arms. Was there ever an anthem, either for the Croatian community or for the Croatian republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not have an anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then moving to Article 12, I'll read that article out. "Until such time as the elections are held and the bodies of state authority appointed, in accordance with the provisions of this decision, the duties of state authorities shall be performed by the bodies of the authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Until such time as the president of the republic is elected this duty shall be performed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to ask for Article 12 to be shown on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, witness, this decision was adopted on the 28th of August. Would you agree with me that there was a transitional period of a couple of months before all new systems of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna were actually installed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the constituting of the bodies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, this period was somewhat shorter as regards the adoption of the legal instruments of the Republic of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and drafting its own regulations, then this period was a bit longer. So I could agree with you there that it did take several months to adopt all those regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that many former departments and many subdepartments became then ministries under the Croatian republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established, in accordance with the procedure that we outlined and the decisions that were passed, the House of Representatives appointed the members of the cabinet at the proposal of the prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mr. Jadranko Prlic's title changed from president of the HVO to prime minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the new title that Mr. Prlic held was the president of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I think you testified to that on Monday or Tuesday, but is it correct that after the establishment of the Croatian republic that decrees were no longer labelled as temporary legislation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the new legislative body, called the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, for the most part passed laws and those laws were not provisional in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would now like you to look at document 1D 01778. And this is again a document that you saw also in chief which is in fact the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that you used in drafting the founding document. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you to go to Article 2 in the first addendum, which is addendum 1, constitutional agreement on the union of the republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's on page 5 in the English version. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So Article 2 reads: "The flag and the coat of arms of the Union of the Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be determined by a law adopted by the Assembly of the Union." Now, this -- would you agree with me that here there's no mention of a flag or a coat of arms that -- for each separate republic within the union, but that they're talking here about a flag and a coat of arms for the union, and that nowhere else in the text there is mention of a flag or a coat of arms for each separate republic of within the union?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 2 that you've just quoted stipulates that there is a possibility and indeed an obligation on the part of the federal parliament to determine the flag and the coat of arms of the union of the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that the -- that it is quite logical to speak only of the flag and the coat of arms of the union of the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina since this document deals with the issues related to the internal structure and the symbols of this union of the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The issue of the symbols of the constituent republics is quite logically in the jurisdiction of those constituent republics, and this is something that has to be stipulated in the fundamental legal instruments establishing those constituent republics of the union. And in this context it is logical that the issue of the symbols of the republics is not included in this constitutional agreement about the union of the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And to support this claim let me remind you that the federal agreement in BH, the Washington Agreement, made it possible even for the cantons to have their flags and coats of arms, and they do have them, all cantons in Bosnia and Herzegovina today do, and the entities were also entitled to that as were -- as was the state. So this is the situation that we have today and it is quite usual, in fact. The issue of determining the symbols of the republic is in the jurisdiction of those republics, and this is something that they have to stipulate in their own legal instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, sir, do you think that the union would have agreed that each republic would have also their own flag, their own coat of arms, and their own anthem? I mean, clearly those are all symbols which represent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. It calls for speculation. There's nothing in the document, there's nothing in the negotiations, and I will be on re-direct pointing out to a document that we've seen here in court on previous occasions on the constitution law of the Republic of Bosnia, which was done by the Muslims in Sarajevo, where indeed in Article 8 it calls for the coat of arms, flag, and anthem of the Republic of Bosnia shall be defined by law. Regrettably the gentleman has not sat through every session, does not know the documents, and so I would ask that we move on for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 4 of this document on addendum 1, and this reads as follows: "Neither the Union of the Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor any one of the constituent Republics, shall retain their military forces, while all forces in the existence on the day of the entry into force of this Constitutional Agreement, shall be progressively disarmed and disbanded under the supervision of the United Nations and the European Union." So here we see, you know, an important provision in which they say that the republics shall retain their military forces. Now, I would say that that is quite an important provision, and I don't see anything of that back in the document establishing the Croatian republic. Could you explain us why that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to something that you said and set matters right. The article says that neither the association of the republics nor any of the constituent republics would be keeping their own armed forces, which is exactly the opposite of what you state in your question to me. If that is the question, then I have to say that the article is abundantly clear. It tells you that the republics -- neither the republics nor the federation will keep their armed forces. As for the Croatian side, the Croatian side agreed to such a solution by signing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well -- okay, well let's move on then again to the day that the Croatian republic was established and proclaimed. I think you've stated that you were present at the meeting. Is it correct that this meeting was held in Grude? You don't have to look for the document. I would just ask, the meeting in which the foundation -- the foundation meeting of the Croatian republic, was this held in Grude, this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show Exhibit P 01032 which is a -- and it's going to be shown in Sanction, which is a video of this action, official proclamation of the Croatian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Perkovic, you may look at it and I'll ask you some questions afterwards. And maybe if you could, I'll ask you beforehand to see if you can identify the persons that are behind the table in the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there is a transcript, but it's -- there is also subtitles in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I've asked you to look at, you know, the persons also behind the front there. Could you identify the persons who were seated at the front table -- at the front table?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see President Boban and then Mr. Perica Jukic, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Srecko Vucina, to the right of Mr. Boban is the writer Andjelko Vuletic I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We have a video still here. So is the person next to Mr. Prlic, all the way on the right hand, who would he have been? If you look at this still, which four persons are we seeing here from left to right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban, Perica Jukic, Jadranko Prlic, and Srecko Vucina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
