utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we also heard that there was an anthem sung. Which anthem was sung?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard the national anthem of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina called "Lijepa Nasa Domovina," Our Beautiful Homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the flag that was hanging behind the table? We'll see if we can find it. There you go.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber has any questions on this video, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one question on this anthem, Mr. Perkovic, is that also the anthem of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the declaration of independence by the Republic of Croatia, Croatia adopted this anthem as its own state anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, finally on this topic could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 04626, and this will be in your binder again, Mr. Perkovic. P 04626.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is a publication in the bulletin of the HVO IPD, which is obviously Herzegovina operational zone. And it's entitled: "Finally Masters in our own Home."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the title. I don't know how it was translated but in Croatia it means: Finally on our own ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You have the document in front of you or are you looking on the screen? It's also in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You might want to look at the hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the number is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you about this agency that issued this report, it's called the IPD. Is it -- is this correct that this was a press agency of the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. IPD [Realtime transcript read in error "IDP"] was one of the information departments, and this was part of the defence department but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just read out one sentence from the second paragraph of this article. It says: "... the Croats took a step forward yesterday. The equality of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina of the three constituent peoples can only be realized on a territory where the Croatian people will be the majority and where they will establish their state ..." Would you agree with what's been written here, that the Croats took a step forward and that they ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at all these activities against the background of the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan, the main objective which was to stop the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to find a new internal organization for Bosnia and Herzegovina, then in that case to me this definitely constitutes a step forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a technical point, if you look at lines 19 and 21 of page 49, you will see that on page 19 the question refers to IPD, whereas the answer mentions IDP, and I suppose it should be the same both times and that would be IPD. Would you agree, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, IPD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, let me ask you to look at the last sentence of this article and I just want to ask you how you interpret this last sentence. It reads: "Indeed the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna is the guarantee of both the preservation of the principles and integrity of the borders from the Helsinki Act and for the inviolability of the territory of the motherland of all Croats, the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of the Helsinki Act, I suppose the reference here is to the basic act, establishing to all practical intents the OSCE. This act takes as its starting point the fundamental principle of inviolability of state borders, and it says that these borders cannot be changed by force, by an act of aggression or anything like that. Against that background, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna believes that as far as the interests of the Croatian people are concerned, the guarantee would be precisely the inviolability of its borders, and the inviolability of its borders probably means the inviolability of the borders and the guarantee for those borders neighbouring on the Republic of Croatia. I don't know just by way of an example how the HZ HB could guarantee the inviolability of the border between Croatia and Hungary, for example. The reference here is to the shared border, the border between the HZ HB and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have just a few more topics to discuss with you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before you go on to the next topic, I do hope with that previous question regarding where he was talking about the taking the step forward that the Judges will keep in mind the rest of the paragraph that wasn't read because then it puts it into full context. I noticed that the Prosecutor wanted to end the question with the word "state," but then if you go on it gives a fuller explanation. And so I do hope that that hasn't been lost in the Trial Chamber's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, let's move to another topic which you were asked some questions about in direct which was Exhibit P 02679, which is the 8 June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, nothing escapes the notice of the Judges, and before we move on to another document I would like to have your feelings about the part of the text dealing with Croats in Muslim prisons. We have figures here that supposedly were given by Mr. Pusic and in relation to the number of Croat or Croatian detainees. Do you have any comments about these figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, regardless of a person's ethnicity, I personally always opposed the idea that anyone, regardless of their religion or ethnicity, should spend even a single hour in detention as long as they were detained because of their race, religion, or ethnicity alone. Throughout the war as a human being, I spared no effort to help my friends who belonged to other ethnicities and of course they could always confirm this for your benefit. Not only did I oppose this, I openly resisted these phenomena, and I fully sympathize with these people who spent even a single minute in detention or in prison on these grounds alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to this document a number of civilians were detained in Mostar, 450 of them, and 110 soldiers were detained in Mostar. As far as I understand, these people were Croats. If the Muslims indeed were holding these Croats in Mostar, where were these people actually detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the specific locations at which these people were held in detention. I didn't cross the demarcation to the other side of Mostar at the time, not even once. I never went to East Mostar, but I do know something that was generally known to everyone living in Mostar, and something that emerged at the end of the war. At the end of the war on the side controlled by the HVO there remained between 5.000 and 6.000 Bosniak citizens. On the opposite riverbank under the BH army control there remained no more than 500 ethnic Croats. These are facts. How did this state of facts come about? Now that is probably a different story, and a long one to boot. I really don't know anything about detention centres in East Mostar or around East Mostar and I don't know where these people were being held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I note something in your answer, something that could be of relevance. You say that at the end of the war in Mostar west, in the area controlled by the HVO, there were between 5.000 and 6.000 Bosniak citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wish everyone not to miss an element which characterizes the taste of this pamphlet, and it's the very last page where under the title of Auschwitz a "joke" of the worst possible taste. I will not put it into the record because it really -- it shows that this is a pamphlet, this is polemic, and I think it should be kept in mind when we consider this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this document, I would like to point out for the transcript that there is probably an error at the beginning at the top of the first page. I quote in English: [In English] "The creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on the 28th August, 1999." [Interpretation] Obviously the date is not the proper date, it should read "1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you wanted to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, could I ask you to look again at P 02679. This was a document that was shown to you also in the examination-in-chief and it concerns the decision on the establishment of the county military prison in Gabela. Now, sir, if we read the part under item 2 it says: "The Decision comes into effect immediately and will be published in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna Official Gazette." And I think your evidence was in direct that you can't recall that this decision was ever published in the Official Gazette; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it your evidence that all decrees and regulations adopted by the HVO were all published in the Official Gazette or did the HVO have the authority to decide not to publish certain decisions or decrees for reasons of security or even other justification existed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All decrees and decree laws were published in the HZ HB Official Gazette. As for any other laws and regulations passed by the HVO of the HZ HB, they were published whenever the enactments themselves referred to their imminent publication in the Official Gazette of the HZ HB. We see one of these decisions of a lower order, lower than a decree. That's what I mean. And it reads that it will be published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And then in this same document we see that there is nothing indicating that the document is a confidential one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I tried to understand your answer but just -- I don't -- I'm not sure exactly what the answer is if I interpret it right. Are you saying that all laws and enactments were always published in the Official Gazette or did there exist laws and decrees that were not published in the Official Gazette, either decisions or laws or decrees? In this case we're talking about decisions. Would all decisions always be published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about decisions that had this actually written in them, the fact that they would be published. There was an obligation to publish such decisions in Herceg-Bosna's Official Gazette. As for the first part of your question, were all the decisions and decrees always published, the normative enactments were not published regardless of their nature or type as long as they were classified strictly confidential, secret, and marked out as such. Confidential, normative enactments, clearly marked out as such were not published in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna. All other such documents, wherever it was indicated that they would be published, were eventually published in the Official Gazette. I hope I've now made this abundantly clear. Specifically talking of this decision, it contains a remark which makes it clear that it would be published in the Official Gazette. It follows from there that there was an decision to publish this in the Official Gazette of the Croatian of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Perkovic, it's now clear to me. Was the publication of the decision in the Official Gazette a requirement for the decision to come into force? In other words, if this decision wasn't published in the Official Gazette would it have done -- would it have done -- would it have not then be a decision that would be coming into force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any decisions containing any indication that they would be published and that were eventually not published, such as this one, obviously manifest a legal drawback or a legal defect, if you like, based on which I am led to conclude that their application, at least until such time as they had been published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer is missing the verb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You may have to repeat the answer because I think a part of it was not translated into English, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is a decision containing this indication that it would indeed be published, and this is the sort of decision that we are looking at in this case, and when this decision is not published in the Official Gazette, for me, in my opinion, this decision manifests a legal defect of such magnitude, in fact, that it cannot be considered to be legally valid or applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But as you say, it's in your opinion. Do you know whether there was anywhere in the HVO Rules of Procedure a provision which actually said that if a document wasn't published in the Official Gazette the document would not be a valid decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there is a norm that stipulates this specifically, but jurisprudence or legal practice in all countries including the former Yugoslavia before this time states that no prison was ever established without a decision being published previously in an Official Gazette. If that is not the case then we face a situation where we have some so-called secret prisons, and we saw how much that causes an uproar when we learnt about some secret prisons in democratic countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move to another topic. Witness, I think you've said so in chief as well, is it correct that you had your office in Mostar throughout the period of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a part of an office because if you have an office that is maybe 6, 7, or 8 square metres, up to four people sat there, the whole of the commission that I headed and I shared this office with first two and then three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, where was your office located in Mostar, and I think you moved at one moment offices? Can you explain where it was initially situated and where did you move afterwards and when did you move?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the Bosniak-Croat conflicts in Mostar broke out, my office was in the Ero hotel, it used to be a nursing home in Mostar. And since this nursing home, or rather, this hotel was at the front line dividing the two sides, when the conflicts broke out the office was moved to Bijeli Brijeg to the premises of the meteorological office in Mostar. And after that while, but at any rate before the conflict in Mostar ended, the office was moved to once again to the Projktant building in Mostar, that's at Mostarska avenue. So we moved the office three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Perkovic, on the 9th of May when the conflict broke out in Mostar, were you in Mostar around that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day after the conflict broke out I was not there. As far as I can recall, it was at the beginning of the weekend, it was Saturday, and I've already indicated that I spent all my weekends in Livno so that I was not in Mostar when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was the first time you came back into Mostar after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I got back on Monday morning, the 10th or the 11th of May, I'm not sure. It was a Monday morning, that's because the working day started, and I didn't know where to go because there was gun-fire in Mostar. I ran into a colleague of mine and I asked him about the situation. He told me that it was possible to get to the hotel, that it was not a problem at all. And since I didn't know in any way that the conflict would -- that the conflict would broke out, all of the stuff remained in the hotel, nothing had been taken out. And Mr. Zubak and I took my car, we went there. He faced the same situation. So we just went there to pick up all the stuff, the papers, the stamps, and so on. And as we got out of the hotel my car was hit by two or three rounds, but fortunately we escaped unharmed. So for a few days we were not in Mostar because there was this state of semi-chaos, semi-anarchy, because communication -- there was a communication breakdown and of -- various offices were trying to find some provisional premises in all kinds of buildings. This was just make-shift accommodation which didn't even provide the basic facilities to make it possible for the administration to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, is it correct on that day that you were in Mostar, the first day you were in Mostar after the 9th of May, that you actually noticed that there was a group of 200 and 300 people guarded in the Velez, and this is evidence you gave in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this is outside the scope of direct examination, and if he wants to go into this area, assuming that it is relevant, that it would be non-leading questions. That's the format based on -- or as it was inspired by Federal Rules of Evidence 611b.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, during the examination-in-chief no mention was made of the 9th of May. This is a new issue you are addressing. Do not put your questions about this as you have done. Please put your question in a neutral manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, on that day did you pass the Velez stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I couldn't get to the office that was in the Ero hotel, so we were in Bijeli Brijeg, and those who are familiar with Mostar know that the road to Bijeli Brijeg leads -- goes by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you notice anything when you were passing by the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not getting any English translation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed a group of people, of persons. I was in a car as I passed by and I saw them from the car. There may have been about 200 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know what -- did you later learn what happened with these 200 people that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this was the same group of people because I said that I passed them by in my car, but later on there were reports in the media about a group of people who were placed in isolation in the stadium. So in the media, in the public, there was mention of a group of people of that sort. Now, whether this was the same group of people, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was referred to in the media? What kind of group of people were these? Were these civilians and what ethnicity had these people? Do you know what was said about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all those years it is difficult for me to recall, but the reports in the media differed depending on their affiliation. The explanation in the Croat side was that these were -- this was a group of citizens who were put in isolation in that period for just a few hours in that place. I assume that the other media, international media, painted a different picture. From where I am now and from where I was at the time, I cannot say whether one or the other is a true version of events. But I do know that there was fighting going on in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 1D 01666, 1D 01 -- it's probably at the back of the binder, 1D 01666. Now, sir, these are minutes of the 38th Session of the HVO government. And again, if we look at the persons present we can see your name appearing there as well. Would you agree that you were present at that meeting, it's dated the 17th of May, held in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just read out the third paragraph of this under item 1. It says the following: "Support was expressed for the activities of the Office of Expelled Persons and Refugees which has been active since the first day civilians were relocated from Mostar to the former Military Gymnasium and Heliodrom, after the commencement of combat activities in Mostar ..." And then it continues and I'll read out also the last part of this paragraph where it says: "... civilians were relocated for safety purposes." Now, sir, do you recall this topic being discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the minutes, as far as I can recall, the discussion was about the refugee crisis in general and that included these areas, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it talks about civilians being relocated to the Heliodrom. Was it the understanding of the people present at these meetings that these were both Bosnian and Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that this was all about civilians and the need for all the civilians who were in the areas directly affected by combat activities should be evacuated from that area regardless of their ethnic background. And by the way, let me just remind you, now that we're on this topic, that this statement that is also contained in the minutes also indicates this, where it is stated that all the elderly, the women and children were returned to their homes in the areas where apparently it was possible to do so, for these people to return. And there's also another fact, that a certain number of these people - and it is underlined here - crossed to the left bank of the Neretva, East Mostar, at their own request. That's what it's underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me as it is stated here that the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees had a role in relocating these persons to the military gymnasium and the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What persons? I'm sorry. Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What persons are you talking -- are you asking me about? I told you in my reply that I -- you were asking me about civilians, that -- and I said in my reply that I think that some of the civilians, as you can see from the minutes, were returned to their homes and that a certain number of persons were sent to the other part of the town at their own request. We're talking about civilians, the elderly, women and children. So I think that if you're asking me about civilians that I gave you my answer as to what happened to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I may have said persons, but I could have said civilians as well. So if I would phrase it that way, would you agree that the Office of the Expelled Persons and the Refugees had a role in relocating the civilians of Mostar to Heliodrom and the gym?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I've already said. The issue of the relocation and accommodation of civilians was something that the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees was dealing with, and when it came to the transfer of people from areas affected by combat activities, I think that this was the job that this office was supposed to perform and they really should have done it, it was their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the period that followed after May when the conflict had broken out and you were still in Mostar, did you ever notice civilians in West Mostar being evicted from their houses? Did you ever see incidents of that happening in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you ever witness people looting houses in West Mostar during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this period I worked in Mostar, but in my free time after the end of the office hours and during the night I did not remain in Mostar together with the other officials or some of the officials. I was staying in the hotel in Citluk. I never saw any looting of the apartments during the day, although of course I heard about such incidents, cases when this happened, but mostly at night-time. It is quite clear from the context of my testimony that it is not by accident that the HVO HZ HB initiated talks with the municipal HVO in Mostar in an effort to improve the security situation and to prevent the crimes that were being committed in wartime. And unfortunately, we've also seen that crimes of this kind happened also after the war. But it is very difficult when you have the whole town, which is virtually the zone of operations, to keep everything under control, but it is quite obvious that continuous efforts were being made to improve the security situation in Mostar to put things under control, among other things, by preventing such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one other question. Did you notice that the mosques in West Mostar were either destroyed or damaged in the period after May 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know how many mosques there were in West Mostar. I do not exactly frequent places of worship, but I did notice that all seven mosques in the town where I lived, Livno, and I was there, or rather, that throughout the war the mosques remained unharmed and they were all intact, and that was also part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Livno is the second-largest municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We're not talking about Livno here. I specifically asked you about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mostar is concerned, I did notice that there was a mosque in West Mostar, in Balinovac, it's a neighbourhood there, that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I have just one final matter to discuss and then we're done. Could I ask you to look again -- and this is not going to be in your binder because it was an exhibit presented to you by Mr. Karnavas. It's 1D 01912, and maybe we can either have it on the e-court or maybe a hard copy can be provided to Mr. Perkovic. Now, Mr. Perkovic, this is a letter that Mr. -- that you were shown from Mr. Jadranko Prlic addressed to Mr. Cot, the commander of the UN peacekeeping forces in the former Yugoslavia dated the 4th of December, 1993, and it's now on the screen. Do you recall your evidence on this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just quote what you stated in relation to this document. And this is a quote from page 99, lines 10 to 17, of 2 September. "And in this letter the steps that the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna intends to take are also listed, and what I find to be quite important here is that in this document there is explicit and clear condemnation of the events that had affected the overall struggle of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina quite adversely, such as the crime in Stupni Do, the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, and so on. So this is one of the first documents where this is mentioned in those terms, where this is this determined condemnation of all of that." Now, do you recall this evidence, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, why did the Croatian republic government feel a need to or perceive a need to strongly condemn these matters?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because primarily this is an attitude that stems from a certain civilizational level. In Stupni Do a certain number of civilians fell victim in this operation and obviously the Croatian Defence Council was responsible, or the units that took part in it were responsible. And also to my mind any crime must be condemned. And in this context there should have been moral strength to condemn those crimes, and I think that this act on part of the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, sir, on what basis were these condemnations made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably on the basis of the information about the events in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the letter which is in front of you, in the fourth paragraph it talks about: "A detailed investigation has already started of the events that have justifiably caused disapproval and shock of the public and abroad." So it talks here about a detailed investigation. Do you know whether there were ever any conclusions reached in relation to these investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know how and in what way those investigations were brought to a conclusion. It wasn't part of my job to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that -- for Stupni Do you've stated that HVO forces would have been responsible. Does that -- the same account for the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you see in this document is a condemnation of the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar. As you said yourself, the HVO launched an investigation to look into that incident. I told you in my reply that I was not aware of any results. As I am not aware of any results, I can't tell you that the HVO is responsible or not responsible for this. I am simply not aware of the investigation results.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perkovic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a break now. Mr. Karnavas, how long will you need for re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I would like at least 15 minutes, Your Honour. Now -- I was under the impression that we were going to be terminating at 12.30 or was it 12.15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible? Yes, it's possible. So try and make sure that we can finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. If I could -- we'll distribute right now the documents. I just have a few documents to go through. And I'm going to ask the usher to kind of move as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first document I'm going to show you is 1D 01436. Okay, 1D 01436, and this is in picking up from -- it should be the very last document, perhaps, in your bundle. This has to do with the question that was put to you by the Prosecutor where he asked you whether you would be surprised that the Muslims did not want to sign on to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan because it might create a state within a state, words to that effect. Looking at this document which has been already presented in court through previous witnesses, if we see that this is dated 28 September 1993, it's titled: "Constitutional Law Constituting the Republic of Bosnia." If we look at the very last page we see the name of Miro Lazovic, president of the BH Assembly. Can you tell us whether Mr. Lazovic would have been the president of the BH Assembly at that time, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were you aware that while you and the others were drafting documents on the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Sarajevo there were efforts to draft a constitutional law on the Republic of Bosnia? Not the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the Republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan, I personally found it logical that something similar would be done in Sarajevo along the same lines as what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We don't have time to go through the entire document but just for the Court's edification Article 5 it says: "The Bosnian language shall be the language of the official use in the Republic of Bosnia." Do you know whether there was a Bosnian language at that time or a language known as Bosnian, an official language?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was the Croato-Serbian, Croatian, or Serbian language that was being officially used in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnian language -- the Bosnian language is not something that is officially encoded or enshrined in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 8, again because you were hammered away at, and I use that word because there were relentless questions on this issue, we see Article 8 that: "The coat of arms, flag, and anthem of the Republic of Bosnia shall be defined by law." Is this any different, sir, than what is contained in the document establishing the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Are not the Muslims in Sarajevo trying to do the very same thing for which you folks are being condemned by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That seems pretty leading, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it is leading, but I can go step by step.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 8 of this draft decision is entirely identical to the constitutional decision on the coat of arms and the national anthem in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's switch topics, and I want some clarification on this, and again it's for the Court, and I'm going to be referring to a question and answer that you gave yesterday, it's on page 31909, and it dealt with the issue dealing with the first decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the one that you had reviewed and had issued an opinion when you were in Sarajevo. And you were asked a question: "In your opinion did the drafters of this decision intend to include the full territory of the municipalities as part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?" Now, I'm going to read you your answer and I'm going to ask you to kindly explain part of the answer because it's -- I'm not sure what exactly is being said here. I think I know but we need to make sure it's clearly on the record. "As far as this" -- this is your answer. "As far as this decision is concerned, the entire territory of these municipalities was included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in terms of the political party organizing because there were municipal party structures based in individual municipalities and the areas they covered as political party structures were identical to the areas of municipalities themselves. And I'm referring to HDZ structures." Can you please explain that part of your answer, especially when you say "in terms of political party organizing because of -- there were municipal party structures. I think we covered it early on in this trial with other witnesses, but please explain that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the decision on the founding of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was adopted, the party blueprint was copied in terms of how the HDZ was organized at the time, I'm talking about the political party of course. In other words, all those municipalities specified in Article 2 were municipalities where the HDZ had a municipal board with the exception of two municipalities: Trebinje and Skender Vakuf. In those two municipalities there were no HDZ municipal boards. There was a smaller-scale form of party organization which I think was called the local branch. Whenever the political leaders of those municipal boards met, when they adopted the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it was precisely on this basis that the municipalities were enumerated from which the people came who attended those sessions of the municipal boards. As there were no municipal boards to speak of in those two municipalities, you have the parenthesis there, specifying that what is meant here is the local branch, Ravno in the case of Trebinje and Dobratici in the case of Skender Vakuf. That is why I am saying with absolute certainty that what's at stake in Article 2 in the sense of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna being established is something that draws upon the fact of the personal presence of, I believe, 16 presidents of those municipal boards and two presidents of the local branchs at that meeting. And that is based on what an extrapolation was made as to the area that makes up the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I'm going to switch to another topic. On September 1, 19 -- 2008, we had a discussion where you told us that after going back to Sarajevo you met with your minister, I believe it was Mr. Nikolic, you made a proposal, and he directed you to a functionary, someone at a much lower level, and you indicated that the gentleman was Sead Dautbasic I believe, I'm not pronouncing it correctly, but can you confirm that that exactly what you said, and I'm quoting from page 31635, line 7.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just run this past you in a single sentence. Mr. Nikolic told me to go to the head of the legislation department of the BH government and his name was Sead Dautbasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we're not going to go into that, but I want to show you now document 1D 02953, and this has to do -- we're going to tie it all up because you were asked a series of questions regarding the constitutional court. If you could look at that document it's dated 9 April 2002. Again, for the record, 1D 02953. This is a decision to elect the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's the last document, Your Honours, I apologise for the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decision to elect the president of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Article 1, Dr. Ismet Dautbasic, candidate of the party of democratic action, is elected the president of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, you were in Sarajevo, you know the players, it's a small country. Is this individual, Dr. Ismet Dautbasic who is being appointed by the Muslim party, the SDA, to be the president of the constitutional court, is he related to the same functionary, the -- that you were directed to by the minister? And I'm talking about Sead Dautbasic. Are they related?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they're brothers, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I point this out again for the Trial Chamber's -- because on page -- when we had Mr. Akmadzic he talked about nepotism and this is another example in our estimation and also because of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas should not be give evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm merely helping the Trial Chamber by pointing out the relevancy, Your Honour, but I'll take that to heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber -- can you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you're asking a question, then you're showing the document, that's all well and good. But then you are drawing the conclusions yourself. That's why Mr. Bos stood up, to object. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we just reconfirm the number because I'm not finding this 2953. Sometimes it didn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 1D 02953. This was introduced today. We brought this out today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay, that explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain how it is that a political party is appointing the president of the court, and might that explain perhaps how it is that the constitutional court reached its decision or, better yet, took the steps that it took - and you told us during your testimony that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not informed - might that explain something, and if so what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is again a very leading question and I think Mr. Karnavas should not ask leading questions in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman did indicate that the proper procedure was not followed by the constitutional court. We have now a link, two brothers involved. We have somebody from the SDA appointed as president, and might this -- I'm asking him might this have something to do with the manner in which the constitutional court abused its discretion in reaching that decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my mind, the whole question of legality of any actions taken by the constitutional court is questionable from the moment that, for one reason or another, legal and legitimate representatives and members of that court walked out, those who used to be in those positions up until the war erupted in Sarajevo or over the first months of war. To my mind, the question of the legality of that court as a whole is highly questionable, including the position of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, and I'm switching but it's sort of related, to 1D 02458, and this has to do with the whole issue of the Sarajevo solution of creating these -- the groups, the various districts. This document here, we see this is a letter to Mr. Pasalic, and it's coming from the Ministry of Energy, Mining, and Industry. We don't have time, regrettably, to go through all of it, and -- but if we look at what is being asked, especially when it talks about industrial production and then at the last paragraph in that section it says: "The overall coordination of the production of armaments and military equipment in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is directed by the state authority for the production and transportation of armaments and military equipment, which is organized within the Ministry of Energy, Mining -- within the Ministry of Energy, Mining, and Industry. It is our belief that the state authority would be able to conduct its activities on the territory of the district Mostar with greater ease if one of its experts would be permanently based in Mostar ..." And if we go further ahead of this particular letter it appears that they're asking Mr. Pasalic to take certain actions. Can you tell us how is it that the minister for mining, energy, and industry is contacting the head of the Muslim army in Mostar to take certain political actions -- or what would appear to be political actions? Is there an explanation? Is that how government worked normally, where a ministry would be directing the army to do something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you would greatly assist the Chamber if you would tell us to which question of cross-examination this relates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It certainly relates to the whole issue of -- if you recall, Your Honours, there were -- there was a document shown concerning the establishment of regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of districts, okay, and of course if we go through the documents because the next document is 1D 1949, then the next document of course that I would be presenting is 1D 021 -- 22112, which is Dr. Jadranko Prlic's answer to that, and then followed by 1D 01210, which is a document that we have already seen. What is being argued by Dr. Jadranko Prlic is that you have certain ministers undermining Izetbegovic in a sense in trying to force the military to take actions in establishing these regions, and he's saying that there is essentially a coup d'etat. That you have certain ministries, and of course when you look at the personalities involved, clearly they're on the extreme elements of that particular party, and it's calling into question how is it that Izetbegovic is at the international level pursuing these peace negotiations based on various models and at the same time ministries such as mining and industry are telling the military leaders at the local level to essentially force political situation -- decisions and that's the whole basis. So it ties in to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't have time, but I do wish for the gentleman to at least comment on this very briefly if he can. And I'm -- for instance, 1D 014 -- 1949 from the deputy minister of defence, and here he's talking about: "According to a government decision, the minister of defence in cooperation with the minister of justice and minister of interior, adopted instructions on implementing regulations on the organization and functioning of the authorities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." If we stop there and then fast-forward to 1D 01210 by Pasalic himself, Arif, and Demirovic, here he's talking about on page 2: "In recent days we have noticed certain tendencies from Sarajevo from your vicinity which are rather worrisome. Some ministers and commanders are sending instructions on the establishment of legal organs of authority, the renewed operation of enterprises, and other activities which essentially mean the creation of organs of authority parallel to the Croatian ones. In addition, some of our 'hotheads,' when they visit Sarajevo, assert that BH must be united and indivisible, that there can be no provinces as if you and we would be against that." Provinces of course are being negotiated. "These instructions are being sent to the army while we, the regional leadership in the party, we are being completely bypassed. On perhaps the regional committee, Safet Arif and in my own name I call -- I can say that this is irresponsible and unrealistic and consequently very dangerous." Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is Mr. Karnavas asking a question to the witness or is he addressing the now Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm addressing the Court. Again, I'm entitled -- there's an invited response. So, Your Honour, this is what I am trying to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I had accepted your response one page ago, Mr. Karnavas, and you just went on and on. That was not called for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware you were fully satisfied with my explanation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we need to have a short break because we've been sitting for more than an hour and a half. I also believe that Ms. Alaburic wants to address the Chamber with respect to next week. I hoped that we would be able to complete our hearing at half past 12.00 but we have to continue after the break. We'll have a 15 minutes break and we'll continue for 15 minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, do you have any further questions to put to the witness because we stopped abruptly, so I don't know if you finished or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that these documents are not rejected by the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, in their deliberations. So I just pose one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, as I understand it during the break you had an opportunity to look at the documents concerning this particular issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go now over the first document 1D 02458, we see again that this is directed to Mr. Pasalic and it is from Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. Now, were you aware -- did you know Mr. Mahmutcehajic and were you aware of the position that he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic was the minister for industry and energy in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I also think that he was the deputy president of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would that make him number 2 to Mr. Izetbegovic in the party in SDA politics?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the party had several vice-presidents, but he was clearly one of the most influential figures in the Party of Democratic Action in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look under paragraph that's number 1, and we see sort of in the middle of the paragraph it says: "We are convinced that basic and developed forms of legitimate and legal authorities in the southern part of our Republic - with a special significance of the army system in parts of the Ministry for Internal Affairs - must be the pillar for resurrecting and developing all other bodies of the government." When we're talking about the southern part of the republic, what part is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the constitutional name of that part of the republic is being avoided here, and that name is Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on to the second page under a)2, power-plants on the Neretva river, we see where in the middle -- towards the end of that paragraph it says that: "In accordance with that we demand that a plan for personnel change be prepared and that technical aspects of the plants be strengthened in accordance with state governmental interests. To that extent it is of vital importance that all the workers in the Regional Command Centre in Mostar be advised that all actions commanding the electro-energy potential contrary to the suggestions and orders of the legitimate authorities are directed against the basic interest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same is to be brought to attention to all the executive personnel of the plants." Now, I guess one question is: How is it, to your understanding, how is it that a minister of -- for mining -- for energy, mining, and industry is now demanding the commander of the 4th Corps, Mr. Arif Pasalic, the commander, that is, to take in action? What authority -- under what authority is he acting, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't think that he had those powers. The usual procedure for the communication and for transferring regulations down the chain of command, in accordance with the provisions that were in force at the time, was for those task to be issued by the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Supreme Command of the armed forces or the BH army, and then to go down that chain of command to lower levels of organization, but this was not the case here. But the relevant jurisdiction of the army is particularly questionable if you have a public company such as the Elektroprivreda, the power supply company of Bosnia-Herzegovina which also ran the hydro-electric power-plants on the Neretva river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look under paragraph number 2, this is on the very last page, it says: "In light of the situation in the southern part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we suggest that the established communications systems be used for all communications. We believe that all existing authorities must act towards legitimate and legal centre, while all forms of political and administrative arbitrariness should be considered treason." And of course we see who signed it and then we also see who this is direct -- who is copied. We see that it's the minister for internal affairs, the Commander-in-Chief of the army, Sefer Halilovic, and the coordinator of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Now, can you give us any explanation why a minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. I believe that Mr. Karnavas is mistaken but correct me if I am wrong. He says that the letter was sent for information, but if you looks at the letter in B/C/S you see that there are stamps, signatures, and in the English translation of the text we have the name of those who signed the document, Mr. Jusuf Pusina signed for the minister for internal affairs; we have the Commander-in-Chief Halilovic; and then we have the coordinator, Mr. Ramo Maslesa. So the impression we get from looking at this document is that it's a letter sent between ministries or from various ministries sent to Mr. Pasalic. Can you please clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the letter that the three ministries, represented by the appropriate persons who signed this letter, sent to the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army, Mr. Arif Pasalic, giving him clear instructions as to how to proceed regarding the functioning of certain segments of government and life in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for that clarification. I was looking at the English version and that had escaped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I know that you're not -- this may be outside your functions at the time, but Mr. Pasalic is the commander of the 4th Corps; Sefer Halilovic was the commander. And now he's being -- Mr. Pasalic is being directly addressed by the minister, even though it's co-signed by Halilovic. Is there any explanation or can you tell us based on this Mr. Pasalic is subordinated to this particular ministry or to the government and is outside the chain of command, I mean, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, his only function was the commander of the 4th Corps in the chain of command, so he was subordinate to the Supreme Command of the BH army. And obviously, since three people, representatives of various ministries, signed this letter the intention is to reinforce and to give weight to the instructions, guide-lines, that are given to Mr. Pasalic, although in my eyes he was not authorised to take any action outside of the military sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I notice that this communication is not addressed to anybody -- anyone from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO HZ HB. Can you draw any conclusions as to why, for instance, Mr. Mahmutcehajic would want to be having these sorts of communications with -- within the Muslim community but not with the Croats, given that you have Izetbegovic running around claiming to be the president of all three constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this calls for speculation. I don't think the witness can answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a ruling, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you provide an explanation for this or would it be speculation from your -- from you if you had to answer, as stated by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is quite clear to me that this is primarily lack of confidence or trust in the institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and efforts to reinforce those institutions and competencies in that area that were in a certain way there to degrade those institutions in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the next document 1D 01949, this is dated now the 24th of February, 1993, and we see the subject: "Instructions to implement regulations on organizing and functioning of the authorities of RBH in times of war." And now this comes from the deputy minister of defence, and this is to all district secretariat of defence. And now you -- just to go through this because you indicated that -- and you were asked questions about information coming to and from Sarajevo. We see from the very first paragraph: "Since there is no -- since there is -- since there is an information blockade in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was not possible to send all Secretaries of Defence the Official Gazette of RBH containing regulations and other documents ..." Would this confirm what you were trying to tell us earlier on your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I was talking about, and let me just remind you, bring your attention to another sentence in this letter where it says this is why many regulations could not be implemented. So I think that this sentence illustrates in a very striking manner all those things that I was telling you about, about the municipal elements and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Then it goes on to say: "According to a government decision," it doesn't note which decision, it says, "The Minister of Defence in cooperation with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of the Interior, adopted instructions on implementing regulations on the organization and functioning of the authorities in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war." Now, again -- I mean, you knowing the political culture and how the system operated, it says: "According to a government decision, the Minister of Defence ..." Why would the minister of defence be put in charge of implementing these regulations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document in the context of what we've been discussing we can see that this conclusion of the government was not acted upon, if any such conclusions existed at all, because it says here that this is the job of the Ministry of Justice and Administration. And in the document that we looked at a little while ago, I don't see that the minister of justice and administration actually signed this guide-line or this instruction together with all the other people there. So if we're talking about the issue of jurisdiction or competence, then it is quite clear that this is an instruction sent to the commander of the 4th Corps and that there is a mix-up because the institutions that were supposed to sign this document did not sign this document, whereas it was signed by representatives of other ministries and the contents of the instruction goes beyond the purview of their institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We go to 1D 02212, this is dated 27 February, a few days later, and this is a statement from an emergency session of the HVO HZ HB, and of course I don't want to go through all of it but if we look at under number 1 we see where Dr. Jadranko Prlic is saying: "Simultaneously with the incidents involving the BH army, some ministers from the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina acting independently or in association with parts of the BH Army Military Command, are arbitrarily taking over the competences of the legitimate authorities and are making moves that objectively represent elements of a classic coup d'etat ..." I'll skip the rest of the paragraph though it's rather interesting and go on to number 2. It begins by saying: "The HVO of the HZ HB is warning the general public, the Muslim people, and their political leaders that such attempts by the coup forces within the legitimate leadership of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are made, as a rule, when the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and leader of the Muslim people, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, is out of the country participating in internationally supervised negotiations for a peaceful settlement of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This fact tells a lot." Again I'll skip parts of it, and then I'll just make reference to perhaps number 5. It says: "The HVO of the HZ HB views as very harmful and dangerous attempts by such forces to blame the Croats or to apportion the blame between the Serb aggressor and the Croats, although everyone is aware of the contribution the Croats and the HVO have made, not just in the joint liberation operations but also in providing assistance to Muslim units in different parts of the Republic. The Command of the BH Army Tuzla Corps, which has received considerable defence aid in recent days despite difficult access through Central Bosnia, might testify to this." And then he goes on to say in number 6: "In light of the latest developments, the HVO of the HZ HB has decided to close the border crossing in its territory towards the Republic of Croatia for all cargo and people in the service of BH Army. This decision has been made in consultation with the Regional Board of the Mostar SDA and will be rescinded in consultation with them." Now, if we look at the previous two documents, and we look at just the parts that I'm referencing to the statement made by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, can you draw any conclusions as to what is happening and what is this response about, particularly keeping in mind that you were at the time participating in some of the meetings as we saw?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this letter signed by Mr. Prlic we can see a conclusion that is not difficult to be drawn, and that is that some military structures within the institutions of Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were meddling in the affairs of the civilian authorities contrary to the valid laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this context this letter, in a way, wants to draw attention to this type of conduct and indicates is measures that will be taken in this context. Let me remind you that not long after this letter was written and those measures taken, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina replaced the supreme commander of the BH army, and among the explanations officially provided for his removal was that he had taken upon himself powers that were outside of those vested in him as the commander and that he was actually meddling in the affairs of the civilian authorities. We're talking about the removal of Mr. Sefer Halilovic. So in other words, Mr. Izetbegovic and the Presidency soon after this letter, a few months later, actually corroborated the suspicions voiced in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, if we go to the very last document 1D 01210, this is a letter co-authored, it would appear, by Mr. Demirovic and Mr. Arif Pasalic, and it's dated 20 February 1993. Of course this is a few days before Dr. Jadranko Prlic's statement but after, of course, the initial letter that we saw from Mr. Pasalic on the February 14 on the -- I'm sorry, the letter from Mr. Mahmutcehajic to Mr. Pasalic. Here in this letter we see Pasalic responding directly to the president, not to Mahmutcehajic. And of course I want to direct your attention again to the second page in the last part, where I read earlier where it says: "In recent days we have noticed certain tendencies from Sarajevo from your vicinity which are rather worrisome. Some ministers and commanders are sending instructions on the establishment of legal organs of authority, the renewed operation of enterprises, and other activities which essentially mean the creation of organs of authority parallel to the Croatian ones. In addition, some of our 'hotheads,' when they visit Sarajevo, assert that BH must be united and indivisible, that there can be no provinces as if you and we would be against that. These instructions are being sent to the army, while we, the regional leadership in the party, are being completely bypassed. On behalf of the Regional Committee, Safet, Arif, and in my own name, I can say that this is irresponsible and unrealistic and, consequently, very dangerous." I won't go on. The letter has quite a bit of information. But from this paragraph that I just read, tracing back now the documents that we covered, that is, the original letter from Mahmutcehajic, 1D 02458, and then later on the instructions that we saw that were dated 24 April 1993 from Bisic, 1D 01949, is in your opinion Mr. Pasalic addressing the issues that Mr. Mahmutcehajic, the minister, is addressing him? In other words, is Pasalic addressing Izetbegovic to the issues that are being addressed to him by Mr. Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this will call for speculation. I really don't see how the witness can give an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The witness was there. He knows the players, he knows the events; he didn't come out of Mars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, like in the previous case, Witness, this letter which might have been submitted to you during the proofing or now, on the basis of this letter, will you have to speculate or do you have a more solid basis to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Preparing for my evidence here I had an opportunity to read this letter, so I can speak about this letter in this context. In the course of my testimony I also spoke about some other documents which I was not aware of at the time when they were passed or issued, but I acquainted myself with them at a later stage. So I speak about this letter in this context and I can give you my answer because I'm familiar with the contents of the letter, if you allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer would be this: This letter in a way confirms all the suspicions that were contained in the letter written by the president of the HVO HZ HB about the attempts by certain majority elements in the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that area to take initiative and to take measures that go beyond the competences that they had in accordance with the regulations valid at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that answer, Mr. President, I have no further re-direct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and his future endeavours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Perkovic, on behalf of my colleagues, on behalf of Judge Trechsel who left the courtroom a few minutes ago, I would like to thank you for coming here on the request of Mr. Prlic's Defence, and thank you for having helped us to establish the truth. I wish you a safe journey home, and I wish you all the best in your job in the ministry. I'll ask the usher to escort you outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please allow me to thank you and your colleagues for your concern for me, for giving me your attention, for giving me the time to be allowed to contribute to building the truth about this unfortunate time. Thank you. I would like to also thank the Defence and the Prosecution for their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we call it a day I think that Ms. Alaburic wanted to take the floor. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I just wanted to ask a clarification about the witness who is due to be heard next week, this is the witness called by Mr. Prlic's Defence and by the Petkovic Defence. In such situations the practice was for the first Defence to conduct the examination-in-chief in full and then to have the cross-examination and re-direct if necessary, and then the next Defence that called the same witness goes on with its case. I was wondering if we will follow the same practice next week. This is very important for our preparations, first of all, my preparations, but I'm sure that the same goes for Mr. Prlic's Defence, and I would also like to note that we have been proofing this witness separately. So I don't know what topics would be dealt with in the cross-examination, the part of Mr. Prlic's Defence. If you need any further clarifications, both Defence teams stand at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the table that was submitted to us by Mr. -- raised via his counsel, there would be four hours for in chief and in the table I could see that yourself had scheduled two hours for your direct examination. As you rightly pointed out there are several options. The first one would be having Mr. Karnavas starting with the -- with direct examination, then you would be also conducting direct examination; and if necessary, the others would be asking questions. And in the cross-examination the Prosecutor would base his arguments on the basis of the two cross-examination -- the two direct examinations; or the other option: Direct by Mr. Karnavas, cross possibly, cross by the Prosecution, and then we start again Ms. Alaburic direct examination, the others, and the Prosecution. I have no preference. It is as you wish. It would be interesting to know how Mr. Karnavas feels about this. Is there any problem for you if after you -- Ms. Alaburic conducts the direct examination or would you rather have the Prosecution cross-examining and after that Ms. Alaburic would be conducting direct? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For once, I was hoping that you would ask the Prosecution how it felt and what its position would be because it does complicate their cross-examination as well. Here's one more indication of how thoughtful I am of the Office of the Prosecution - I want to be on record on that one. I do think that it may be a little bit easier if one direct followed the other and then cross-examination is conducted. I think for efficiency purposes that's how I'm familiar with back in my jurisdiction, that, you know, the direct would be done and then there would be cross-examination. That would prevent any overlap, but again for me it doesn't make a difference one way or the other. That's why I think it might be important to hear from the Prosecution, but again if we're running into time problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, good afternoon. I'm always very appreciative of Mr. Karnavas's efforts to protect the interests of the Prosecution. I thank him for that. On this one I think Mr. Karnavas and I in fact are in agreement. I think it would be more efficient and productive if any direct examinations are conducted first and then the Prosecution can conduct one set of cross-examination. There might be interconnections, they might be inter-related, and it might be better to take it all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I think Mr. Karnavas should go ahead first with his chief and that should be unrelated to the Petkovic examination. Not only the OTP but all the other Defence teams as well, including Mr. Petkovic's Defence, have the right to cross-examine a witness, this witness in question, based on the Prlic in chief. That was the practice that we adopted in the case of two previous witnesses. Bozo Kovacevic cross-examined a witness who was to become his own witness on the following day but this was redirect. If I may just make another suggestion. I have taken into account the interests of the OTP and I'm trying to look at this case as a whole. Perhaps we could take the following course of action. Maybe the OTP should be allowed to cross-examine after both of our chiefs and after all of the crosses that the other Defence teams might have. I think that would safe-guard the right of each Defence team to cross and we would also make the OTP's job easier and simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're suggesting is as follows: Direct examination by Mr. Karnavas; after this, the other counsels cross-examine if necessary; after which you conduct your direct examination; the other lawyers, if necessary, cross-examine; and eventually there is cross-examination by the Prosecution. Is that your proposal?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What remains is perhaps a small problem concerning the re-direct. So in one word precisely as you say, but then the issue of the re-direct arises. Personally, I don't oppose the possibility that I should do my re-direct after everything else if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, re-direct is not a small problem, it's a big problem and it's a big right that is owed to the party that brings the witness. If this indeed -- and I don't wish to get into debating this issue. From a strictly technical point, the witness is being called by two parties and you can't have it both ways. When the one witness calls the party you're going to treat him as an adverse witness and shortly thereafter you can treat him as a friendly witness. I can understand the utility in having the flexibility of asking cross-examination questions in certain areas and then switching to direct examination in others. But the bottom line is that I think if you do it in the manner in which is being suggested by Ms. Alaburic, we're going to run into some technical problems, it's going to take a lot longer, and I certainly don't want to be in a position where I have to do my re-direct examination, followed then by God knows what the direct examination is going to be, and then I have to cross-examine a witness that I just did the direct on. Because then it essentially becomes a second re-direct. Now, I don't know how the Prosecution feels about this, but I do think from a technical standpoint it is best to get all the direct examination out of the way. I can't imagine that there's something that needs to be covered both -- twice, on two different occasions. That would be my preference. I'm not pushing for one way or the other. I will do, you know, whatever instructed, but I think it makes better sense to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What's your response, Mr. Scott, to Ms. Alaburic's proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to confess, Your Honour, I'm not sure I appreciated the exact variance or variation that she proposed, but I think our views on this after having heard the discussion over the last few minutes is, again, that all the Defence questioning either -- whether it's called direct or cross-examination, and the Chamber knows the ongoing issues and arguments about that, but that all Defence questioning of the witness precede the Prosecution's cross-examination; and then of course any appropriate re-direct would follow the Prosecution's cross-examination.
