We're not trying to interfere with the right to re-direct, but that would then follow the Prosecution's cross-examination. But we would prefer for the Prosecution's cross-examination to be all one go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just put in a reaction to what my colleague Mr. Scott just said. This might strike one as a logical line of reasoning, but so far in situations such as these the Prosecution did not make this request; rather, they would cross-examine a witness for the Prlic Defence and then they would cross-examine -- do another cross-examination several days later when the cross-examination was taking place based on the chief done by the Praljak Defence. I see no reason at this point in time to change the established practice. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that each Defence has a right to cross-examination, a right which no Defence should under any circumstances be denied. I really do not know at this time what subjects Mr. Karnavas will be dealing with or, indeed, whether the subjects will affect my client in any way at all. However, may I call your attention to the interview that Mr. Prlic gave to the OTP, and this is part of this trial, it's in evidence, and then also the statement that sparked off the Prlic Defence. I have every reason to believe that the evidence of this witness would also be used in order to pin some actions that are considered to be questionable to the army and to the commanders, in which case I must also be granted a right to cross-examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me be very clear on this point. I'm trying to avoid the issue. It is very clear that the Petkovic Defence wishes to insinuate, and in fact they're trying to prove that based on one particular decree the executive authority of the HZ HB was actually giving operational decisions and, in fact, holding secret meetings. Of course, we categorically deny that, that has never occurred, that's not how to read the law, and this has been a constant attempt by Ms. Alaburic to place the executive in an operational aspect of the military. Be that as it may, once they call -- this is their witness as much as it is ours. Now, they can't have it both ways. Either they give up their direct and just simply cross or he is their witness and accordingly they treat him as their witness. It is nonsense to say that on the morning session I'm going to treat him as a hostile witness and ask questions because he's a hostile witness -- not hostile emotionally but for the purposes of cross-examination, and in the next session be all lovey-dovey with the witness because it is their witness. This is ludicrous and trial advocacy 101, any judge would tell you in an adversarial setting that you can't have it both ways. Not only does it undercut your own witness's credibility. How can you impeach the witness one moment and the next moment try to get -- elicit information that upon which you're then going to say to the Court that he should be trusted on the direct examination but not be trusted on the cross. It just doesn't make sense. Now, I'm trying to be as reasonable as I possibly can be. I don't know this whole notion about the statement. We're running a defence. They've had the documents. They've had our plan. We have made the witness available and brought him in a day early. We are giving the witness to them without participating. They can have him all day tomorrow, even though we're paying for him to come here a day early because the Tribunal won't pay for it. So I don't see all of this -- and, you know, if they want our cards on the table they're right there on the table, they're right there, they have our documents. But this notion somehow that there is some nefarious and sinister motive behind this in which now we have to treat this witness somewhat differently than the others, for me it's inconceivable. I simply do not understand this process. And it could very well be that we have two different systems colliding, the civil law system with the adversarial system, a lawyer who is very well-versed in the adversarial system versus a lawyer who is not so well-versed, and maybe they're trying to find creative ways, but this is not the approach that we should be taking. The Prosecutor is right, he is entitled to conduct his cross-examination at the end of all of the testimony from this side of the bench. I support him on that because it makes sense, and to say anything otherwise would be illogical. And then at what point do I do my redirect? I mean, there are all these issues that are not being taken into consideration by this approach and we can't have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I must admit that I could understand Mr. Karnavas or take him seriously had he not allowed the Praljak Defence to cross-examine in a situation where these witnesses had a witness that they shared. If my colleague Mr. Karnavas had taken the same course of action at the time, I would have believed this to have been out of professional reasons and out of principle and because he was well-versed in the adversarial system, or any other system, including the procedure applied before this Tribunal. Since, however, Mr. Karnavas failed to do so then, I don't think anyone should mind that a Defence would cross-examine a witness that in a matter of days will become its own witness. Secondly, as for the statement in the first paragraph in my learned friend's reaction, Mr. Karnavas's reaction, that I was systematically trying to show how the government was making operative military decisions, let me now paraphrase Mr. Karnavas and say this: I'm truly sorry that Mr. Karnavas is sitting here in this courtroom all this time without following the trial, therefore leaving himself unable to accurately quote my questions and the context of my questions because my questions leave one thing perfectly clear at any time. This is not about operative military decisions by specific military operations carried out by specific military units, but the involvement of the government and everyone else in issues that have to do with the country's defence. That is why I believe Mr. Karnavas's reaction to be entirely inappropriate and I do wish to advise the Trial Chamber of the following as well. Just last week I sent a list of subjects or topics that I might be raising on cross-examination to the Prlic Defence. I also enclosed a list of exhibits that I will be using with this witness. The reply that I got was that I would get a reply to next Monday. To this very day I have received not a single word by way of reply to my previous e-mail. Based on this I can hardly conclude that the Prlic Defence is showing any great desire in relation to that mail that had to do with the substance of the chief, and that is why I can hardly be expected to believe that I can in any way cooperate with the Prlic Defence in terms of proofing this witness. I believe the Trial Chamber should know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to bring this but I will call my colleague to be representing less than the truth. She was told verbally that she could have access to the witness. She was told by my colleague. E-mails were sent. And I find it rather shocking that an officer of the court would stand here and make such representations. Secondly, with respect to the Praljak Defence, it was a statement, it was a written statement on a very discreet issue. It is no secret that these Defences are not getting along. I perfectly understand where she's going, just as she gave us her documents, we gave her our documents. We have made the gentleman available. She even indicated that the other Defences can meet with the gentleman in her office. So this notion that somehow we didn't respond is pure poppycock. Now, let's stick to the issue. How are we going to proceed on Monday? For me it doesn't really make a difference. I'm not going to try to treat the gentleman as hostile one moment and non-hostile the other. This is purely an issue of logistics and how to treat a common witness. That's the point. You can't treat a witness one moment as a hostile witness and the next moment as your witness; that's the point. And it's for the Judges to make a determination how they wish to proceed, and from there on we're at your disposal, we'll do as we're ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will consider the matter, the Bench will consider the matter. I can't tell you what the Chamber has decided because we need to refer the matter to our fellow Judge who is not here with us, but there is one thing where I agree. The Defence can't call a witness who would be then considered as a hostile witness. I share Mr. Karnavas's point. It's a matter of logic. I've always believed that cross-examination of a witness by -- a Defence team, Defence team of one of the other accused, is something that is a bit tricky. But that's the way we proceed here, pursuant to the way it's done in English-speaking countries, in common-law countries. The Judges will consider the matter and we'll tell you how we'll proceed on Monday. It's a matter of deciding who is going to go first, what's going to happen first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just two sentences. I can't just sit here and listen to Mr. Karnavas's allegations that I wasn't telling the truth. Every single word I said is backed by our e-mail exchange and we still keep all of that. Secondly, I consider it to be entirely inappropriate for Mr. Karnavas to be addressing me as a "she." I consider that to be entirely unacceptable in any tradition, the Anglo-Saxon tradition, the common-law tradition, and any other tradition you may might care to cite. Thirdly, I wish to draw your attention to our exchange with regard to certain motions by the OTP. There was a lot of exchange going on, and we said that no analogies should be drawn between cross-examination on the one hand and hostile or friendly witness on the other as such. These two subjects are to be kept apart. In the Anglo-Saxon tradition one can cross-examine a witness who is not at all hostile to one's client. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica stood up but I had not seen her.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I merely wanted to contribute to this. I know where this conflict arises from and I do not wish to take sides at all, but I do wish to say one thing at this point in time, it has indeed been our established practice, at least with witness Buntic, because I do share some witnesses with the other Defence teams so I believe it to be entirely logical that I should be allowed, for example, if another Defence wants to -- a part of their examination with one of my witnesses because these are all complex witnesses who will give evidence about a whole range of subjects covering a long period of time and encompassing a great many documents. It could easily be the case that another Defence calls a witness, or that I call the witness, and then I cross-examine the witness as a friendly witness but then maybe I may not broach a subject with a witness and I may wish to add to that or raise something else. We have three or four proposals in terms of procedure. And what we've been doing so far, I think there are sufficient grounds for a ruling to be made that will leave all the parties happy now as in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask you all to tell Mr. Jukic that he'll probably have to come back on the following Monday. We don't be able to complete his testimony next week. I don't think so. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know everyone is anxious to leave the courtroom, and I'll be very short, but if I can have just one minute to the Defence 20, let me just say that -- because I don't think this is going to be the last time this issue comes up. I expect there's going to be future discussion of this and similar issues. Some of the comments that have been made in the last half-hour directly relate to a number of issues the Prosecution has been raising in a number of respects about the proper conduct of cross-examination of friendly witnesses, and all of these issues are interrelated, and we'll come back to it in the future, Your Honour, but I just want to note it for the Chamber's direction. These are exactly some of the concerns that the Prosecution has raised about the way in which the Defence is allowed to conduct what's being called cross-examination of an indeed friendly witness, and today this afternoon there's been references to how they can be friendly one hour and hostile the next hour. And therein lies some of the problems that the Prosecution has tried to raise before. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to adjourn because it's high time we did so. I wish you all a very pleasant weekend. I hope to see you all, all of you, here on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
